name: Bilberry
summary: Bilberries are small, dark wild berries of northern Europe, related to the blueberry but a different species. This page lists what people say bilberries do; each claim can be checked against the research when you choose.
inIt: Bilberry (Vaccinium myrtillus) is not the cultivated blueberry (Vaccinium corymbosum). A study that compared them found cyanidin the main anthocyanin in bilberry and malvidin the main one in blueberry, and the highest total anthocyanins in the skins of blueberries.
Bilberries hold anthocyanins, the pigments behind their colour, and are used widely in juice and food in northern Europe, according to a 2023 review.
The UK food table (CoFID) has no entry for bilberries, so this page shows no measured nutrient amounts. Its blueberry entry is a different species and cannot stand in for them.
Most trials of bilberry used standardised extracts, for example 240 mg a day for 12 weeks, not the whole berries eaten as food.
processing: Extracts are a different thing from the fruit: the eleven trials in a 2025 meta-analysis tested bilberry supplementation, not berries eaten as food, so their results do not carry over to the whole fruit.

whoShouldBeCareful.with: Picking wild berries and not sure which species
whoShouldBeCareful.note: Bilberry (Vaccinium myrtillus) and bog bilberry (Vaccinium uliginosum) are different species. A 2024 review says many European countries hold a strong prejudice against bog bilberries and a few poisonings were reported between 1906 and 1944, but the supposed toxicity remains unproven. If you are unsure which berry you have, or feel unwell after eating wild berries, talk to your doctor.

cautions: A 2025 study in 12 countries found fox tapeworm (Echinococcus multilocularis) DNA in 5.4 percent of shop-bought strawberries and 7.3 percent of blueberries from seven European countries where it occurs. It did not report bilberries separately, and it noted that food has not been shown to raise infection risk much.
unknowns: Whether eating whole bilberries has the effects reported for extracts: the trials mostly used standardised extracts.

Whether bilberry changes blood sugar or blood fats: a 2025 meta-analysis of eight trials found no clearly significant change in fasting glucose or total cholesterol, and a borderline one for HbA1c (p = 0.06).

Whether bilberry helps eyes: a 12-week trial in 109 adults found that 240 mg a day of extract relieved a measure of eye-muscle tension after screen work, and the people in it were healthy adults, not patients.
